title: Keeping Actions safe

story: A teammate merges a small PR titled [FE] Use `useQuery` in the projects table. GitHub squashes it, so the title becomes the commit message on main. Frontend CI goes green on main, and a small workflow posts the result to the team's Slack channel, as it does after every build on main. Today the post says: Commit Summary: [FE] Use  in the projects table. One word is missing, and the workflow's log explains why: useQuery: command not found.

Bash tried to run a word from a PR title as a program. This time it was harmless, a function name in backticks. But PR titles are typed by people, and soon they are also written by agents that read Jira comments anyone can write. This workflow runs on our own runners inside our network, in a job that can read a Slack secret.
hook.question: How can text in a PR title become a command, and how do we write workflows that always treat such text as text?

read.h: The runner pastes, then bash runs
p: Here is the step from the story, as it is in fcp today. It looks like it echoes the commit message, but the order of events matters. Before the runner starts bash, GitHub evaluates every ${{ }} expression and pastes the result into the script as plain text. Only then does bash read the script, and bash cannot know which characters came from you and which came from a commit message. Backticks and $( ) inside double quotes mean 'run this command and use its output', so the word useQuery became a command.

This is script injection, and it is the same family of bug as building an SQL query by gluing strings together. A harmless title produced a missing word. A title like Fix typo"; curl …; echo " closes the quote and adds a command of its own, which then runs on our runner, inside our network, with whatever that job can reach. Any text a person can type is untrusted here: commit messages, PR titles and bodies, branch names, issue and review comments, and the inputs of a manual run. Values that GitHub sets itself, such as github.sha or github.run_id, are safe, because nobody can put shell syntax in them.

code.text:
- name: Extract Commit Summary
  id: commit_first_line
  run: |
    COMMIT_SUMMARY=$(echo "${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_commit.message }}" | head -n 1)
    echo "commit_summary=$COMMIT_SUMMARY" >> $GITHUB_ENV

notes.text: The expression is replaced by the commit message before bash runs, so the message becomes part of the program.
Writing text that an attacker controls into $GITHUB_ENV is risky too: it sets environment variables for every later step.

read.see:
COMMIT_SUMMARY=$(echo "[FE] Use `useQuery` in the projects table" | head -n 1)
echo "commit_summary=$COMMIT_SUMMARY"
--- output:
bash: line 1: useQuery: command not found
commit_summary=[FE] Use  in the projects table

p: The fix is small. Move the expression out of the script and into an env: entry, then read the environment variable inside the script. GitHub still evaluates the expression, but now it puts the result into the variable MESSAGE, and bash receives the text as a value. A value is never parsed as code, whatever quotes, backticks or semicolons it contains. Quote the variable, "$MESSAGE", so that spaces stay part of the value, and use printf '%s' rather than echo, which treats some values, such as -n, as options.

Two more lines make the step safer. permissions: {} gives the job's token no access at all, because posting to Slack needs a webhook, not GitHub. And the summary goes to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, where only later steps that ask for it can read it, instead of $GITHUB_ENV, which changes the environment of every later step.

code.text:
permissions: {}

jobs:
  notify-slack:
    runs-on: fcp-runner-set
    steps:
      - name: Extract Commit Summary
        id: summary
        env:
          MESSAGE: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_commit.message }}
        run: |
          COMMIT_SUMMARY=$(printf '%s\n' "$MESSAGE" | head -n 1)
          echo "commit_summary=$COMMIT_SUMMARY" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

notes.text: No scopes at all. The job only needs the Slack webhook secret, not the GitHub API.
The expression is still here, but as the value of an environment variable. The script text never changes.
printf '%s\n' prints the value as it is, and the double quotes keep it one value.

p: When a step needs both the event's fields and some logic, write it in JavaScript with actions/github-script. The script receives a few ready objects: context holds the event and the repo, github is an authenticated GitHub API client (a later lesson teaches it), and core logs, sets outputs and fails the step. Event fields are read in code as context.payload.<field>, so a hostile branch name is just a string in a variable.

The trap is to paste an expression into the script anyway. const msg = "${{ github.event… }}" is injection again, into JavaScript this time: a title with a double quote ends the string, and the rest runs as code. The small workflow that wakes our CI fixer is written the safe way on purpose. It never checks out code, and it has no ${{ }} inside the script; the only expression, a repository variable that admins set, arrives through env:.

notes.text: Pinned by full SHA, as the previous lesson taught.
A repository variable, read in the script through process.env, never pasted into it.
The event payload is a JavaScript object. Nothing from it ever becomes source code.
Asks GitHub for an identity token for this job. The next section explains it.
Without setFailed, a bad answer from the service would leave the step green.

read.h: Nothing to steal: logging in with OIDC
p: Even with careful workflows, assume one injection gets through some day, and ask what it can take. The worst answer is a long-lived cloud key stored as a repository secret, because a stolen key works from anywhere until someone notices and rotates it. OIDC (OpenID Connect) removes that key. The job asks GitHub for an OIDC token, a short signed JSON document that says, for example, 'this job runs in repo RhinoHealth/fcp, on branch main, in this workflow file'. Each of those statements is called a claim. AWS or Vault checks GitHub's signature and the claims, and if its trust policy accepts them, it hands back credentials that expire within minutes.

A job may only ask for that token if its permissions say id-token: write. fcp's cloud integration tests log in to AWS this way, and no AWS key is stored for them. Their credentials last 15 minutes, so even a leaked one is worth very little, and the role's trust policy decides which repos and workflows may borrow the role at all.

code.text:
permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read

jobs:
  prepare_cloud_environment:
    runs-on: fcp-runner-set
    steps:
      - name: Configure AWS Credentials
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@e1253824e5c10ff9df46874f81ed3ec929e19cfd # v6.3.0
        with:
          aws-region: ${{ inputs.aws_region }}
          role-to-assume: ${{ inputs.role_to_assume }}
          role-duration-seconds: 900

notes.text: Without this, GitHub refuses to create the OIDC token, and the AWS step fails.
The action trades GitHub's token for temporary AWS credentials and sets them for the later steps.
The job can only become a role whose trust policy accepts this job's claims.
900 seconds: long enough for the step, short enough that a leak is almost worthless.

deeper.h: Go deeper: which claim to trust
p: The sub claim looks like repo:RhinoHealth/fcp:ref:refs/heads/main, so a trust policy that matches repo:RhinoHealth/* trusts every workflow in every repo of the organization, including any new repo and any workflow an agent might add. The job_workflow_ref claim names the exact workflow file the job runs in, such as RhinoHealth/fcp/.github/workflows/_cloud-int-tests-reusable-aws.yml@refs/heads/main, even when another workflow called it. Binding a role to a list of job_workflow_ref values means only those files can borrow it.
Vault, the server that holds our secrets, accepts the same token through its jwt login method, which fcp's workflows use with the hashicorp/vault-action action.

lab.title: Inject yourself, then close the door
needs: uv, so that uvx can run zizmor
lab.goal: See a PR title run as a command on your own laptop, then rewrite the step so text stays text, and let zizmor confirm it.

guess.q: A step says run: echo "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}". The PR title is Fix `npm ci` flake. What does bash do?

options.text: It prints Fix `npm ci` flake, backticks included.
options.why: The title is pasted into the script before bash runs, so bash sees backticks inside double quotes, which mean 'run this'.

options.text: It runs npm ci as a command and prints Fix  flake.
options.why: Backticks inside double quotes are command substitution. The title became part of the program.

options.text: Nothing: GitHub escapes special characters in expressions.
options.why: GitHub pastes the text exactly as it is. Escaping is your job, and env: is the reliable way to do it.

follow.say: Make a scratch folder and save a tiny imitation of a runner. Like the real one, it pastes the commit message into the script and then runs bash.
Save the script part of fcp's step exactly as it is written today.
follow.do:
cat > step.sh <<'EOF'
COMMIT_SUMMARY=$(echo "${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_commit.message }}" | head -n 1)
echo "commit_summary=$COMMIT_SUMMARY"
EOF

follow.say: Run it with the title from the story. Read the script bash received before you read the output.
follow.do: node fake-runner.mjs step.sh '[FE] Use `useQuery` in the projects table'
follow.see:
--- the script bash receives:
COMMIT_SUMMARY=$(echo "[FE] Use `useQuery` in the projects table" | head -n 1)
echo "commit_summary=$COMMIT_SUMMARY"
--- output:
bash: line 1: useQuery: command not found
commit_summary=[FE] Use  in the projects table

follow.say: Now a title written to attack. It closes the quote and adds a harmless command of its own, which prints your user name.
follow.do: node fake-runner.mjs step.sh 'Fix typo"; echo "this ran as $(whoami)" >&2; echo "'
follow.see:
--- the script bash receives:
COMMIT_SUMMARY=$(echo "Fix typo"; echo "this ran as $(whoami)" >&2; echo "" | head -n 1)
echo "commit_summary=$COMMIT_SUMMARY"
--- output:
this ran as seanazulay
commit_summary=Fix typo

follow.say: Save a copy of the whole workflow and ask zizmor, the workflow security checker, what it sees.
follow.do:
cat > .github/workflows/notify.yml <<'EOF'
name: "[FRONTEND] - Notify Slack on Main Branch Runs"
on:
  workflow_run:
    workflows: ["[FRONTEND] - CI"]
    types: [completed]
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  notify-slack:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Extract Commit Summary
        run: |
          COMMIT_SUMMARY=$(echo "${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_commit.message }}" | head -n 1)
          echo "commit_summary=$COMMIT_SUMMARY" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
EOF
uvx zizmor --offline .github/workflows/notify.yml
follow.see:
warning[excessive-permissions]: overly broad permissions
error[dangerous-triggers]: use of fundamentally insecure workflow trigger
error[template-injection]: code injection via template expansion
  --> .github/workflows/notify.yml:14:38
14 |           COMMIT_SUMMARY=$(echo "${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_commit.message }}" | head -n 1)
   |                                      ^^^^^^ may expand into attacker-controllable code
error[github-env]: dangerous use of environment file
7 findings (3 suppressed, 1 unsafe fixes): 0 informational, 0 low, 1 medium, 3 high

follow.say: Save one more file now, a teammate's JavaScript version of the same step. You will need it in the Fix it step.
follow.do:
cat > .github/workflows/notify-js.yml <<'EOF'
name: Notify (JavaScript)
on:
  workflow_run:
    workflows: ["[FRONTEND] - CI"]
    types: [completed]
    branches: [main]

permissions: {}

jobs:
  notify-slack:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Extract Commit Summary
        id: summary
        uses: actions/github-script@3a2844b7e9c422d3c10d287c895573f7108da1b3 # v9.0.0
        with:
          script: |
            const message = "${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_commit.message }}"
            core.setOutput("commit_summary", message.split("\n")[0])
EOF

lab.build: Write step-fixed.sh so that the script reads the message from the MESSAGE variable instead of the expression (the fake runner sets MESSAGE the way env: would), and run it with both titles: each must be printed exactly as typed, with nothing executed. Then fix notify.yml: add permissions: {}, give the step an id, move the expression into env: MESSAGE, print it with printf, and write the summary to $GITHUB_OUTPUT instead of $GITHUB_ENV. Run zizmor again. One finding is left, dangerous-triggers on workflow_run: open its documentation link and decide whether it applies to a job that never checks out code.
checks: node fake-runner.mjs step-fixed.sh with the useQuery title prints commit_summary=[FE] Use `useQuery` in the projects table, backticks included.
With the attack title, 'this ran as' never appears; the whole title is printed as text.
uvx zizmor --offline .github/workflows/notify.yml no longer reports template-injection, excessive-permissions or github-env.
The only finding left is dangerous-triggers, and you can say in one sentence why this job accepts it.
In the Fix it step, zizmor reports no template-injection for notify-js.yml.

solution.text:
# step-fixed.sh (the runner sets MESSAGE from env:, so bash gets it as a value)
COMMIT_SUMMARY=$(printf '%s\n' "$MESSAGE" | head -n 1)
echo "commit_summary=$COMMIT_SUMMARY"

# .github/workflows/notify.yml, from permissions: down
permissions: {}

jobs:
  notify-slack:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Extract Commit Summary
        id: summary
        env:
          MESSAGE: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_commit.message }}
        run: |
          COMMIT_SUMMARY=$(printf '%s\n' "$MESSAGE" | head -n 1)
          echo "commit_summary=$COMMIT_SUMMARY" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

lab.fix: A teammate read that shell is dangerous and moved the step to JavaScript with actions/github-script; that is notify-js.yml, which you saved in the last Follow along step. Run uvx zizmor --offline .github/workflows/notify-js.yml. The template-injection finding is still there, now in JavaScript: a title with a double quote would end the string and run the rest as code. Change one line so the script reads the message from context.payload instead, and run zizmor again.
explain: Why does bash run part of a PR title when the title is inside double quotes?
Why is env: MESSAGE safe when the same expression inside run: is not?
If an injection still happened in a job that uses OIDC, what would the attacker get, and for how long?
lab.done: Both titles print as plain text through step-fixed.sh, and zizmor finds no template injection in notify.yml or notify-js.yml.

check.q: Which of these lines inside a run: step is a script injection?

options.why: GitHub sets the commit SHA itself. It is always 40 hex characters, so nobody can put shell syntax in it.
The title arrives as the value of a variable. bash never parses a value as code.
The title is typed by a person and pasted into the script before bash runs, so it can become code.

check.q: A teammate moves a step to actions/github-script and writes const title = "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}". Is it safe now?

options.text: No: the expression is still pasted into the source, now JavaScript; read context.payload.pull_request.title instead
options.why: Injection is about pasting text into code before it runs. The language does not matter; reading the field from context.payload does.

options.text: Yes: JavaScript strings cannot run code
options.why: A title with a double quote ends the string, and whatever follows is JavaScript the attacker wrote.

options.text: Yes, as long as the job has permissions: {}
options.why: Fewer permissions limit the damage, but the injected code still runs, on our runner, inside our network.

check.q: Why does OIDC make a successful injection less damaging?

options.text: OIDC blocks commands that come from event text
options.why: OIDC does not look at your scripts at all. It changes what there is to steal, not what can run.

options.text: There is no long-lived cloud key to steal; the credentials are made for one job and expire within minutes
options.why: The role trusts claims about the job, and the credentials it hands out last minutes, not months.

options.text: OIDC encrypts the job's logs, so secrets cannot be printed
options.why: Logs are not encrypted by OIDC. Its benefit is that no stored key exists to print in the first place.

p: fcp's Slack notify workflow still has the bug from this lesson, and it runs on main on fcp-runner-set, inside our network. Agents make it more urgent, not less: a squash commit's message comes from the PR title, and an agent writes its PR's title after reading text that anyone can write.

The platform's own workflows follow the rules from this lesson. The routine trigger that wakes the CI fixer reads every event field in JavaScript, holds no secrets and proves who it is to the trigger service with an OIDC token. Every repo with workflows gets zizmor, starting in report-only mode, and the Vault role that GitHub jobs log in with is narrowed from 'any repo in the organization' to a reviewed list of workflow files before any agent workflow exists.

tickets.why: The routine trigger: github-script reading context.payload, no checkout, and an OIDC token instead of a secret.
Adds zizmor to every repo; the comment-triggered and workflow_run workflows are the first to read.
Binds Vault's gha-runners role to a list of job_workflow_ref values instead of every repo in the org.
The nightly metrics job logs in to AWS with OIDC to write its numbers.

words.plain: A ${{ }} value that GitHub evaluates and pastes into the workflow as text before anything runs.
When text someone typed, such as a PR title, is pasted into a script and runs as code.
An action that runs a JavaScript snippet with the event (context), a GitHub API client and helpers (core).
A short signed statement from GitHub about which repo, branch and workflow a job is, used to log in without a key.
One statement inside an OIDC token, such as sub or job_workflow_ref.
A checker for workflow files that finds injection, unpinned actions and overly wide permissions.

review.q: Rewrite run: echo "Branch: ${{ github.head_ref }}" so a hostile branch name cannot run.
review.a: env: BRANCH: ${{ github.head_ref }} on the step, and run: printf 'Branch: %s\n' "$BRANCH". The value reaches bash as a variable, never as script text.

review.q: List five event fields a person can type and two that GitHub sets itself.
review.a: Typed: commit message, PR title, PR body, branch name, issue or review comment, workflow_dispatch input. Set by GitHub: github.sha, github.run_id, github.repository.

review.q: What does id-token: write allow, and why is a role bound to job_workflow_ref stricter than one bound to repo:org/*?
review.a: It lets the job ask GitHub for an OIDC token. job_workflow_ref names the exact workflow file, so only those files can borrow the role, not every workflow in every repo.

remember: Text a person typed reaches a script only as a variable, never pasted into it, and a job proves who it is with OIDC instead of holding a key.
